interaction.content: I feel like I’ve gone through two similar things on repeat. The first time was before the student union election in college. Because of this vague feeling, I turned down all activities, and I even stopped doing my work as the counselor’s assistant. The second time is now. I’ve become the city manager I wanted to be, but I still want to resign. My work efficiency is really low, and I feel like I’ve been fooled. I think this goes back to when I was a student: my confidence swelled up because my grades were good, but after I got hit hard, I didn’t know how to heal myself. This problem has already seriously affected my life. I want to know, am I giving up because I’m afraid of failing?

Hi, after reading what you shared, it reminded me of a story. Teacher Wu once talked about a student who was very afraid of riding roller coasters, but after doing dream work, they experienced that standing in a high place could also mean being welcomed, and didn’t necessarily mean being wiped out. I’m thinking your current difficulty may come from the impact of your confidence being shattered back when you were a student, which left you unable to heal yourself. You might be facing some repression in your unconscious. The root may be that the first and second similar events triggered memories in your subconscious, leading to feelings like suppression, panic, and fear. So maybe this current situation has already reached a point where you feel you can’t bear it. Do you want to resign as a way to escape this pressure?
I think I want to get away from this feeling of fear, but I don’t want this feeling to show up again.

I think what you need to do now is first work through your emotions, and then deal with what’s happening in your life. You need to listen to your inner voice and notice the unconscious parts of yourself. That way you can understand what you really want and what you’re missing. At the same time, you need to accept your imperfect self and accept what happened back then, so that those emotions can move and be released, and your experience can shift. If you feel it’s necessary, you can try to find someone to listen to you, but it’s best if the person can really empathize with you, and not listen with judgment, to avoid a lot of inner drama.
I know my inner world is really chaotic, but I don’t know how to handle my emotions well.

If you have time, you can try reading some psychology books, or seek professional counseling. Or you can start from self-empathy, letting yourself understand yourself and building up a more positive inner dialogue. This is a long-term process and it takes patience and time. So try to keep an open attitude toward your emotions, and learn to regulate and manage them yourself.
I don’t know how to accept those negative emotions in myself.

You can try things like writing a journal, getting proper relaxation and sleep, doing something fun, and exercising regularly to really help release the pressure. Also, you can use self-empathy and self-listening to better help yourself face those negative emotions. Most importantly, remember you shouldn’t judge yourself or your emotions, because everyone can learn to accept their own imperfections.
I feel like, apart from being in a relatively good mood, I don’t really have any solid goals in my life right now.

Actually, new life goals don’t have to be anything great or grand. As long as they make you feel happy and fulfilled, that’s enough. You can make some general plans and arrangements, starting from things you’re interested in, and slowly build a more positive attitude toward life. There may be more than one purpose in life, and they’ll definitely be tied to your own values and interests. You can spend more time reflecting, paying attention to yourself, learning to treat yourself kindly, and looking ahead to a more positive future.
I hope I can have more time to take care of myself, but right now the pressure at work is also really high.

Even when life is busy, you still need to keep taking care of yourself. Our body and mind are connected. You need to keep your exercise, diet, and sleep in a reasonable state so you can better cope with work stress. If you feel the pressure at work is too much, you can try to set aside some time to talk with your supervisor or colleagues and see if you can get a better work environment. At the same time, try to build a more balanced attitude toward life and work, so you can truly take good care of yourself.
Thank you for listening so patiently and for your help. I feel unexpectedly much more relaxed in my mood and state now.

You’re welcome. I’m also glad I could do something for you. If you feel the need, contact me anytime, and we can keep exploring how to better handle the challenges and difficulties in your life. I’m sending you my very best wishes.

Ever since I was little, I’ve been really scared of the people around me, because I’ve gone through so much disappointment and hurt. I’m even afraid of interacting with people, I don’t dare to make phone calls or talk. I don’t dare to open the curtains either, and in high school my classmates even said I might have autism. Now my daily routine is just going home and locking the door. I’m really exhausted.

Hi, I hear what you’re feeling. It sounds like you care a lot about what others think and feel, but you’ve been ignoring your own real thoughts and feelings. We need to take care of ourselves first before we can love others. Have you ever thought about telling your family what you’re going through and the kind of support you need inside?
I’m actually really scared they won’t understand me, and even more scared that it’ll put more pressure on them.

That’s a very understandable worry. But you can think about how to put it into words and find a way of communicating that feels right for you. You could also consider seeking some professional counseling to help you with this.
But I don’t know how to even start talking about it.

I can offer a few suggestions. For example, you could first write down your thoughts and feelings, then ask your family to read them carefully and talk with you about it. Or you could first talk about your confusion with someone around you that you really trust.
Okay, I’ll give it a try. But I’m still really afraid that what I do will have a negative impact on them.

First of all, everything has both a positive and a negative side. Right now you’re making adjustments in yourself so you can get along better with your family, and so you can hopefully enjoy the good things in life again. It’s normal to have some discomfort and a period of adjustment in this process; that’s not the same as a negative impact. You really deserve to have this right now—the right to fight for a better life for yourself.
Mm, that’s true. Even though I still feel a bit scared and tired, I’m slowly starting to see some hope.

That’s good, this is a really good start. On the path of building confidence and self-acceptance, we need ongoing persistence and support. I’ll be here with you, walking through this process together.
Thank you, I’m really grateful for your support and encouragement.

My boyfriend is really good-looking and has great presence, he’s like the dream guy in every girl’s mind, but our sex life isn’t good. Every time it ends really quickly. I feel awful and want to break up—what should I do?

Hearing you say this, I can understand how you feel. This is a very personal issue, and you need to think about it calmly and decide carefully. You two can try some new ways and perspectives to see whether your sex life can improve.
We’ve already tried some new things, but it doesn’t seem to have gotten any better.

This might take more time and patience. You can take it slowly and try not to focus too much on how long it lasts. At the same time, you could try bringing this up with your boyfriend directly and talking it through together, so he knows how you feel and what you need.
I’m worried that talking to him about this will make him feel bad or feel like he’s not good enough.

You can talk to him gently and let him know this is something you’re facing together. He also wants your sex life to be richer and more fun, and you’ll need to work on it together to make things better.
Can we try seeing a professional?
Of course you can, that’s a really good idea. You can go to a doctor or a sex therapist, and they can help you find ways to solve the problem.
I really appreciate your advice and support. I’m feeling much better now.
You’re welcome. I’m glad I could do something for you. Everything takes time and persistence, and I believe you two will find a solution that works for you.
Thank you for your confidence in us and for the encouragement. I’ll try to work on this together with my boyfriend.
You’ve got this. I’ll be here rooting for you!
Lately I keep thinking about whether I have an erection or not, it’s like it’s turned into an obsession, and I feel like this is going to affect my life.
Reading this, I feel really concerned. Have you seen a doctor?
I haven’t seen a doctor. I feel like if I did, other people might see me as a pervert.

Focusing on this so much might actually make things worse for you, and it also makes it harder for you to get help. What you need to know is that this is actually very common, and a lot of people struggle with similar things.
That sounds a bit comforting, but I’m still really anxious.
I get it, this kind of situation can make people feel very anxious and distressed. But you need to know it doesn’t mean you have some serious illness.
Thank you for comforting me. I hope I can get a handle on my emotions and behavior.
It’s important to understand that this kind of issue can be worked through with specific treatments and approaches. You could think about seeing a psychologist or consulting some specialists.
I think that sounds like a good idea, but I don’t know where to go for help.
You can look online for contact information for psychologists or specialists. They can help you work through this.
Thank you for patiently guiding me. I’ll try to take some steps to help myself.
I’m really glad I could support you. If you need any help, feel free to reach out to me anytime. I believe you can definitely get through this.

There are a few people in my workplace, more of them are women, who, whenever something comes up, start talking about themselves this and that, saying they just can’t get things done. But the leaders really buy it, and then they’ll say, “Why don’t you do it, if we don’t use you, who else can we use,” and it even looks kind of righteous. I feel like these things weren’t a big deal to begin with, there’s really no need to make such a scene. How should I deal with people like this?

Hello, I understand what’s bothering you, and this really is quite a challenge for you. Sending you a hug. Interpersonal relationships are a very important part of our work. If we don’t have some degree of boundaries, it’s hard to maintain stable relationships. And in the workplace, boundaries are especially important. We need to clearly define responsibilities, distinguish the scope of duties or ways of doing things, so that our own interests are taken into account and we’re not intentionally or unintentionally infringed upon by others. It seems like you want to know how to say no to colleagues who are over-demanding or ask too much. I get your concerns, and I’ll offer a few ideas for you to consider:

Mm, I’m really worried that my attitude and the way I handle things will lead to misunderstandings or hurt other people. I don’t want to affect my professional image, but I also don’t want to offend colleagues or leaders.

It sounds like you’ve already seen the root of the problem, which is how to stick to your own principles and needs while still getting along harmoniously with others. It really is something that takes skill and balance. First, we need to accept a fact: we’re not all-powerful, we can’t do everything, and some things really shouldn’t be our responsibility. For some nonessential requests or extra pressure, we need to find the courage to say no. To be honest, many people find this very hard, and very few are good at refusing others. But we have to learn to say no. That’s the first step in protecting ourselves.
But how do I say “no”? I don’t want people to misunderstand me, or think I’m not a team player or not united with everyone.

That’s a very common concern, I understand. This means we need some strategies and skills so that when we refuse, we can minimize hurting the other person’s feelings. Actually, it often isn’t about how we refuse, but about how we help the other person accept our refusal, and how we maintain appropriate communication and relationships. For example, we can try to avoid saying a direct no, and instead clearly state our current workload, time limits, or other reasons. When we point out these constraints, others can see the difficulty of the situation and understand where we’re coming from, rather than blaming themselves too much or blaming us. This requires us to use a sincere tone and attitude to express our intentions and difficulties.
Okay, I get it. But every time I turn someone down, I always feel really embarrassed, like I’ve caused them trouble or disappointment. How can I overcome this feeling?

That’s very human, but sometimes we twist things in our own minds. Saying no to someone doesn’t mean we’re hurting them. Think about it: if we always give in to others, won’t they become more self-righteous and push us to do more and harder things? Saying no doesn’t mean we don’t care about others. It’s actually because we care about everyone’s time and energy, including our own, that we refuse unnecessary tasks or unreasonable demands. Of course, refusing is also a skill we have to learn. We need to keep practicing so we can gradually build our confidence and independence.
Mm, I think this really will take a lot of time and effort. I’ll try to practice these skills and strategies in my daily life and work. Thank you for your support and suggestions.

You’re welcome, I’m really glad I could help you. Having good relationships with others and protecting yourself is a dynamic balancing process, and we need to keep adjusting and learning. I hope you can soon master the ability to say no, and also enjoy the freedom and balance that comes with it. Finally, I wish you lots of sunshine and happiness in your work and your life.
Whenever I chat with my wife, she keeps complaining about my parents and our child. She feels like people around her don’t like her and she’s unhappy all the time. What should I do?

Hi, I really understand how hard this is for you. First, try to have a good talk with your wife and understand why she feels this way. Let her really feel your support and care, find the root of the problem, and then work together to figure out how to handle it.
I’ve tried talking with her, but I always feel she’s very dissatisfied with my parents and our child. Sometimes what she says is really harsh. What should I do?

What you’re going through is really tough. It might be that she hasn’t fully blended into your family yet, or that there are some things in your family that are making her feel this way. You need to talk with her and listen to how she really feels inside, so you can find where the problem is. At the same time, you can also talk openly with both sides of the family and do your best to coordinate the relationships, so she can feel the warmth and support of the family.
How can I help her change the habit of not being able to accept other people’s criticism?

This is a process that needs time and patience. You can share some healthier ways of communicating with her, like really listening and expressing emotions in a calm, reasonable way, and guide her to build better communication patterns. At the same time, you can also give her more love and support so she feels more confident, and from there becomes more willing to accept other people’s suggestions and criticism.
I’m really worried she’ll stay in this low mood for a long time.

Feelings take time; they need to grow slowly through time and experience. You can stay by her side through this difficult period, give her enough support and understanding, and be like a light for her so she can slowly grow with your companionship. At the same time, you can also encourage her to join some social activities, make more friends, and help ease her mood.
Sometimes I also feel really tired and powerless. What should I do?

As a husband who cares about his family, it’s important to take good care of yourself and keep your inner world as calm as you can. You can find some exercise or relaxation methods to recharge yourself, like yoga or meditation, to help you regain your energy. Also, finding someone you trust or a professional psychologist to talk to can help as well. Don’t forget, you have many ways to seek help and work on these problems.
I’ll give it a try. Thank you so much for your suggestions and your patient replies.
You’re welcome, I’m glad I could help. I hope you can get through this rough patch and come back to share your story with me. I wish you and your family happiness and good health!

Lately I keep feeling like there’s a voice in my head that’s completely different from my own thoughts, even kind of aggressive. I try to control it, but whenever I’m not that busy it always shows up. I’m in a lot of pain, and I’m really scared I’ll make a mistake because of it.

From what you’ve described, I think you might be feeling quite anxious or tense. It’s okay to allow yourself to have any kind of thoughts, that in itself isn’t a problem. If you ever really wanted to act on a thought, your brain would help you by making you think it over again and again: “Is it really okay to do this?” So you really don’t need to worry so much. I’d suggest reducing your stress, talking with someone you trust, or seeking help from a professional counselor. In daily life you can read, keep a journal, do some moderate exercise or other calming activities; these can all help ease anxiety.
But these thoughts and the way I’m acting because of them really scare me. I don’t know if they’ll keep affecting my mood and behavior.

These thoughts probably won’t keep affecting you for very long, because everyone has thoughts like this sometimes, they just handle them differently. Try not to worry too much, and learn to accept yourself—that’s an important step in working with anxiety.
But I don’t want these thoughts to control my life. What should I do?

You can try using some strategies to manage these thoughts, like focusing on lighter, easier things, or talking with other people, and doing activities that help you relax your body and mind. And remember, you have the right to decide how you face your thoughts and emotions.
So, are these thoughts not some kind of illness?
Based on what you’ve described, I don’t think there’s any mental illness. But if you’re worried, I’d suggest going to a specialized hospital or clinic to get it checked out.
Thank you, I’m feeling much better now.
You’re welcome. Anytime you need my help, feel free to reach out. And lastly, remember to take good care of yourself and try to keep a positive and healthy mindset.

For the past three months I’ve been having insomnia. Last month my mom kept yelling at my grandma and yelling at me. My emotions piled up and I felt awful, I broke down crying hysterically. Later I told my mom not to just vent her emotions like that anymore. I have severe depression, and when my mom saw my emotions were really up and down, she held back a lot. But the urge to kill myself that started back then has never gone away, it’s just gotten a bit weaker. I went swimming for two weeks, and during those two weeks I could sleep. Then my period started so I stopped going, and the sleeplessness came back. My mood doesn’t fluctuate that much every day now, but the thoughts of wanting to die have never changed. I still care about my family and friends, but deep down I still feel like life is meaningless, nothing is interesting, I don’t care whether I live or die. It’s really painful. Even though my self‑attack isn’t very strong, deep down I’m still slowly criticizing myself. I don’t know how to change this situation. The people around me all love me, and I’m also very good‑looking, but the thoughts of wanting to die are always there inside me. I don’t know what to do.

Hearing about what you’re going through, I really understand your feelings and your struggle. Many people have gone through similar difficulties. First, please don’t blame yourself. It took a lot of courage to say all this. I’d like to explore together with you some ways that might ease your emotions and help you get through this. Have you thought about seeking professional psychological help? Talking with a psychiatrist or psychologist might bring your heart more comfort and relief. At the same time, healthy lifestyle habits can also have a positive impact on your mood, including regular sleep and wake times, good eating habits, less smoking, and less alcohol.
I’ve never wanted to seek psychological help, but now things are getting more and more serious, so maybe I should give it a try. Also, I really appreciate your company and support, thank you.

You’re welcome. I’m really glad I can be here to support you when you need help. Everyone needs someone to care about them, support them, and love them, especially at a time like this for you. I hope that during this period you can learn to slow down a bit, calm yourself, and take good care of yourself. If you need anything, feel free to contact me anytime.
I’ve been finding it really hard to fall asleep. Do you have any good suggestions?

You can try some relaxation techniques, like meditation or deep breathing exercises. Also, creating a good sleep environment is really important, such as keeping it quiet and comfortable, and avoiding using phones or computers with blue‑light screens at night. I’d suggest going to bed before 10 p.m. and getting up before 6 a.m., and keeping enough sleep time. That can also help improve your mental state.
What you said makes a lot of sense. I’ll try to adjust my sleep habits. I’ll also try to face life more positively. Thank you for your suggestions and for caring about me!

I’m really glad to hear you say that. For you, trying new things actually isn’t easy, and you’ve done really well. I hope you remember that you’re not alone, and these problems are not yours alone. Many people are just like you and need support and care. Please believe that you have the ability and the wisdom to overcome these problems. Remember to reach out to me when you need to. I’ll be here to offer you help.
Saying it out loud makes me feel a lot better. Thank you for giving me courage. I’ll keep working on myself and try to get better.

That’s wonderful. I’m really glad I could offer you some help and encouragement. Remember to often pause and think about the kind of life you want, one that’s full of hope and energy. You’ve got this!
Recently my WeChat account was hacked, and I was scammed out of quite a bit of money.
I'm really sorry to hear that. How are you feeling right now?
I feel really helpless and frustrated.
Hearing how upset you are, I can understand how you feel. Have you thought about filing a police report?
I’ve already reported it, but there’s still no result yet.
Then for now, try to wait patiently. People do what they do, and heaven is watching. I believe in the end there will be a good outcome.
I’m really scared this kind of thing will happen to me again.
I know going through something like this can make you feel uneasy, but try to trust that some things can be prevented. You can protect yourself with some simple safety measures.
You mean, what should I do?
For example, setting a more secure password, turning on two-factor verification, and not sharing your personal information easily can all help make your account more secure.
Thank you for your suggestions, I’ll be careful.
You’re welcome. Safety really is important, and we need to stay alert all the time.
Mm, I get it. Thank you for the encouragement, it makes me feel really warm inside.
You’re very welcome. You can come and talk to me anytime. I’ll be here for you when you need me, and we’ll get through the tough times together.
These days I just can’t stop scrolling on Douyin, it feels like such a waste of time, but I also learn a lot from it, so I’m really torn.

Hi, I get how you feel, because I used to deal with this kind of thing too. I have a few suggestions that I hope might help. First, building a good habit takes sticking with it; after about 21 to 30 days a habit can form. For example, if you read a book every night before bed, after a while it’ll feel very natural to do it at that time. Second, make a plan for each day and put the important things first. After you finish them, tick them off. That way your plan won’t be easily thrown off by outside distractions.
Okay, I’ll try to build a new habit.

Nice. You can start by setting aside a block of time every day just for studying, like reading or learning a new skill. Also, you can try cutting down your Douyin time by setting a limit, for example no more than 30 minutes a day.
Okay, I’ll change my habits a bit and put studying in a more important place.

Yes, studying is really important for you, and it’s a positive investment and growth. In other words, study time is the most valuable time. Once you build this good habit, you’ll spend each day in a way that feels more meaningful and productive.
Thank you so much, your suggestions are really helpful.

You’re welcome, I’m really glad I could offer some help. You can also try looking for other kinds of stimulation and hobbies, like exercise or social activities, to make your life feel fuller and richer. As for Douyin, you can see it as a way to relax and have fun, but try not to let it take up too much of your time. I hope you’ll see some positive changes soon.
Okay, I’ll adjust my state as soon as I can and live each day better. Thanks again for your help.
I’m really happy to hear that. Remember to reach out for support and encouragement when things feel hard. I hope everything goes more and more smoothly for you from here on.
I have a father who is always criticizing me, and I almost feel like every criticism from him is extremely terrifying. I feel completely useless and worthless.

It’s clear you’re really hurt, and because your father keeps putting you down, your inner world has become very fragile. But everyone wants their father’s approval, and that approval is built on respecting your father. The way you see yourself as having no value at all is definitely a problem. And your father’s repeated criticism has gradually made you lose confidence in yourself. It’s even created a negative image of yourself inside, making you feel really bad. My suggestion is that you get one-on-one counseling to help heal these emotional wounds. It may be hard to change your father, but your own wounds can slowly improve through counseling. Once the issues in your heart are worked through, you’ll be able to look at things more objectively and won’t be so affected by what others say.

Thank you for your understanding and support. I feel really depressed, because everyone around me thinks my father is very outstanding, but he’s extremely harsh and dissatisfied with me. It gives me such a headache.

Yes, the pain buried in your heart will keep affecting your life. Remember, your feelings deserve to be taken just as seriously. Don’t forget your strengths; those are things you can use to affirm yourself. Your emotional difficulties are not without solutions; appropriate psychological treatment can help you get out of this low point.
Yeah, I also hope I can be more confident. I feel like if I don’t get other people’s approval, then I don’t deserve anyone’s attention.

It’s very hard to avoid thinking that way, but remember, inside you there is your own most genuine voice. With professional therapy, you can help yourself discover your real value, and then, when the time is right, notice and adjust your thinking patterns. You need to learn to give yourself some affirmation and praise.
Maybe you’re right. I really do need to learn to value the voice inside me. How do you keep your own confidence and courage?

I can share my experience with you: First, accept that you’re not perfect, so we just do our best. Don’t get discouraged because of failure; learn to accept your mistakes, be gentle with your own weaknesses, and don’t compare your shortcomings with other people. Second, face your own emotions, needs, and expectations. Emotional freedom is a basic right we should all have. Third, find things you genuinely like and do them well. Those things can bring you a sense of satisfaction and achievement. Finally, learn to enjoy the little bits of happiness in everyday life, and bring positive energy and a sense of well-being to yourself.

What you’re saying really hits home; these ideas will be helpful for me. But I still feel like there are chains in my heart. I’m always thinking about others first and don’t know how to make myself happy.

Seeing you so caught up in worry, I’m really concerned about your physical and mental health. You need to learn how to look for your own happiness and find ways of relaxing that suit you, like talking with family and friends, writing in a journal, listening to music, or doing things you enjoy. When you start living in your own way, you’ll find you can have your own happiness, and you won’t be putting so much pressure on yourself.

I’ve been married for half a year recently, but my friends and coworkers around me don’t really think highly of my husband. I feel a bit uneasy. He’s very down‑to‑earth, but he’s not romantic and hasn’t really given me any sense of ceremony. I don’t know if my choice was right. Could you help me think it through?

I can understand how you feel. Wanting recognition from the people around you is very normal. Besides what you mentioned, is there anything else that makes you feel uneasy? Even though your husband isn’t romantic, the fact that he can care about you is also very important. You might need to think about where this uneasiness inside really comes from. Do you truly like him? Does he match what you expect from a partner? Love needs more than romance and a sense of ceremony; it’s also about whether the two of you are a good fit.

The reason I feel uneasy inside is that the people around me are always worried I’ll get hurt, and they don’t really approve of my husband. Also, he’s usually busy with work, so we don’t spend much time together. But at the same time I feel he’s very genuine and responsible. I’m really torn.

I get what you’re saying. The worries from people around you may be coming from their care for you, but in the end, whether to be with someone is a decision you need to make yourself. Being with someone suitable requires both sides to compromise and put in effort; try not to demand perfection. You can try talking with him, let him know how you feel and what you need, and see if the two of you can find some common ground.
Sometimes I feel like he doesn’t care about me enough, and our interests and hobbies are different. I’m a bit worried that we might slowly run out of things to talk about.

Your worries make sense. When two people have been together for a long time, it’s natural to feel a bit of distance sometimes, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the love is fading. You two can try some new activities, and slowly adjust to each other while exploring new topics or hobbies together. That might bring some unexpected gains. Try not to give up on trusting him and loving him; when you run into difficulties, you can face them together.
Thank you for comforting me, I already feel much better. I’ll try to have a good talk with him and understand each other’s thoughts and needs.
I’m really glad to hear that. Remember not to ignore your own feelings. Make your own decisions and stick to them. I wish you both happiness.
Mm, thank you for your suggestions. I’ll do my best!
Mm, you’ve got this. If you ever need anything or run into difficulties, feel free to come and talk to me anytime.
Lately I keep feeling really lonely, and sometimes I feel really down. I don’t even know what to do about it.

Hearing you say this, I really feel your sense of disappointment and helplessness. First, you need to know you’re not alone in this; we all have feelings like this sometimes. Second, you could try writing down your feelings and making a list of what you need, so you can see your inner world more clearly. That can make it easier to find a way forward.
So how should I write it?

You can start by writing down your emotions and feelings, including why you think you’re having them. Then write down your needs—what kind of support and care you’d like to receive. Finally, think about what steps you could take to meet those needs yourself.
I’ll give it a try. But I still feel really awful.

I get it. Feeling down is very normal; we all have times like that. But remember, emotions can be adjusted. You can start with small things in your daily life and slowly work on shifting your mindset. Also, sometimes talking to a stranger can actually feel easier and more relieving. You could reach out to some mental health professionals or volunteers to talk things through.
Okay, I’ll give it a try. Thank you for your suggestions.
You’re welcome, I’m here to support you. I believe you will find your own way out. Remember, no matter what happens, don’t give up on yourself. We’ll hang in there together.

My daughter is 16. Back in her last year of middle school, we caught her playing on her phone in the middle of the night. We really scolded her then, and I think we even hit her twice, but we didn’t really go all out. She threatened to kill herself and run away from home, so we gave in, and since then her phone has never left her hand. She’s on her phone at night and sleeps in class during the day. Before the high school entrance exam she crammed for a month and got into a second-tier high school, but she’s still just drifting along. She often just can’t get up and then asks for leave and doesn’t go to school. In the second semester of 10th grade she found a job herself at a friend’s shop, mainly serving drinks and board games for young people and so on. It’s not tiring, the hours are flexible, she often only goes in the afternoon, and after getting off work at midnight she still goes out for late-night snacks, drinking and smoking with friends. She’s basically dropped out of school. Should I take tough measures and interfere? Or wait for her to wake up on her own? It feels like this kind of life really fits her personality: she doesn’t have to use her brain, and she can hang out freely with a bunch of like‑minded friends. The money isn’t much but it covers basic living expenses. So it’s not very likely she’ll wake up because she suffers in society or realizes that without studying there’s no future. What should I do? Whenever she’s late coming home I get worried, anxious, and depressed. I sincerely ask everyone for guidance, thank you!

I can really feel your anxiety and pain. First, I want to say that your daughter may not be doing this just out of rebellion. It might be that some emotional needs inside her aren’t being met, and that’s why she’s showing this kind of resistance. At this point, we need to pay attention to her emotional state and her mental health.
So how should I give her support and attention? I’m really worried about her future.

First, you can try to communicate more with your daughter and get to know her inner world. And when she makes mistakes, parents should choose to guide rather than harshly criticize. Give her a sense of having a role in the family, and offer her support and help with her studies. At the same time, you can also talk with her teachers or counselors to get more help and guidance.
But when I see her wasting time like this and not studying, I feel really sad.

I understand how you feel. But we also need to understand that everyone has a different way of living, and she also needs her own time to grow. We need to respect her choices while helping her look for a life path that suits her. Maybe these experiences are actually part of her growing up.
I’m afraid she’ll do something extreme. What can I do to help her feel less anxious?

To ease her anxiety and depression, you can spend more time keeping her company. Take her out to enjoy the scenery, travel, or join some social activities, and help build warm, close connections within the family and with friends. At the same time, you can help her find some activities she’s interested in, so she can find enjoyment in them and relieve some psychological pressure.
These ideas sound good. I’ll try them out. But I’m still worried that she won’t want to go to school.

If she really feels she doesn’t like studying, you can also consider looking for other career paths that suit her. You can take her to see a career planner and help her find something she truly loves. At the same time, we also need patience and confidence, and to let her slowly find her own direction in life.
Okay, I’ll look for more help and support for her. Thank you very much for your suggestions.

You’re welcome. Whenever you need help, you can come to me. Remember to leave space for both yourself and your daughter for emotional support and growth. Believe that in the future, she’ll move toward a better direction.

I went to the hospital for a check-up the day before yesterday. That day I was also pretty anxious and depressed, in a really bad state, and the result was severe anxiety and depression. It really scared me. I thought I was just moderate, I didn’t expect it to be severe. The doctor prescribed medication. After taking it I feel tired all day, dizzy, my head isn’t clear. Before, it was the tension and fear that made my mind go blank, now it’s the meds causing it. It’s the same kind of suffering, I feel really low. I don’t want to take the meds anymore. I read a bunch of side effects online, but I’m also scared to stop. I’ve taken them for two days. I originally thought counseling would be too slow, and I was still really hurt and in a bad way, so I went to the hospital.
Hearing your confusion, I can understand the anxiety and low mood you’re in right now. But please believe you’re not facing this on your own. I’m here with you now, to explore this together.
Thank you for understanding and staying with me. I really can’t stand this pain anymore.

You don’t have to bear all this pain by yourself. Let’s think together about how to work on your situation. First, maybe you could contact your doctor and ask whether it’s possible to adjust the dosage or switch to a different medication. And remember to tell the doctor about how your body is reacting. That way they can understand your condition better and make better decisions for you.
Okay, I’ll talk with the doctor. But I still have some worries. If the dosage isn’t right, will it harm my body?

Side effects vary from person to person, but if your physical reactions are severe and affecting your daily life, then it’s worth considering changing the medication or lowering the dose. Also, you can try some non-medication approaches, like psychotherapy.
I’ve heard that antidepressants can be addictive, is that true? I’m scared I’ll become a slave to the meds.

Although some antidepressants do have a certain level of dependence risk, not all of them are like that. And if you’re using them under a doctor’s proper prescription and guidance, with reasonable limits, that can greatly reduce the chance of that happening. Try not to be afraid of becoming a slave to the meds—you’re not going to be a slave to them. You’re actively exploring and looking for answers about your own health.
I feel really helpless. I don’t know what I’m supposed to do.

You don’t need to feel helpless, because we’re here exploring this together and looking for ways forward. Let’s think about what you can do, like seeking professional help, or talking with family and friends. There are still many people around you who can stay with you, support you, and walk with you through this difficult time.
I’ve actually been anxious for a long time, and I always feel helpless and guilty. I really don’t know how to face these emotions.

Feeling anxious and helpless is very common, and it’s okay. Try not to blame yourself, because none of this is your fault. We can try to work on these issues through things like psychotherapy. And I’ll be here with you too, supporting you and facing these emotions together.
I’m really grateful to you. Your presence and help make me feel a kind of warmth.

What matters to me is being here with you as you get to know yourself and care for yourself. In this ordinary yet not-so-ordinary process, I believe you can find your own way of dealing with things, and regain the goodness in yourself and in life.

I always feel like communicating with other people is really exhausting. I deliberately try to take care of their feelings, don’t share my own opinions, and then I often say the wrong thing or do the wrong thing.

Hearing you say this, it sounds like you feel really powerless and confused. On the surface you seem to care a lot about other people’s feelings, but you yourself often lack confidence and don’t dare to express what you think. When you were getting along with your parents before, did you also need to listen to them and take care of their emotions? Do you think that might be part of why you feel so passive in relationships now?
Yeah, that’s right. I’ve always been the obedient, well‑behaved child, and I never had the courage to express my own views.

What you’re describing is very understandable, try not to blame yourself too much. I’d suggest you slowly start to notice your own thoughts and feelings, and try to respect and care for yourself, because you’re also a child who’s been overlooked, and there must be your own ideas and voice inside. You can try to share your opinions more often in daily life. Even if sometimes you might say or do something “wrong,” you don’t need to be overly bothered by it.
But I keep worrying that I’ll end up in conflict with other people, and then I might become even more quiet and withdrawn.

Try not to worry too much. Everyone has their own feelings and thoughts, and conflict is normal. Remember, even if you do have conflicts with others, don’t give up on trying to express what you think and how you feel. Only in those moments can you get to know and explore your inner world better.
I’ll try, but I’m really scared.
Feeling scared is completely normal; you don’t need to overthink it. And every time you bravely try to express your thoughts and feelings, you’ll become a bit more confident and mature.
Mm, I get it. Thank you so much for the support and encouragement.

You’re welcome. I believe you can get through this and become a more genuine and confident version of yourself. If you need any help, I’ll do whatever I can to be there with you through each difficulty.

My boyfriend and I have been together since freshman year, it’s been almost five years now. I’ve met his parents a few times, but every time I see them I get really nervous, because they speak Shanghainese and I can only speak Mandarin. What worries me even more is going to see his grandparents over the May Day holiday, because at home they always speak Shanghainese, and I don’t even dare to open my mouth to talk.

Hey, my friend. Listen, you’re not doing anything wrong. Everyone has their own difficulties and fears, and yours are mainly about the language barrier. But if we look at this as more of a “respecting differences while finding common ground” kind of issue, you don’t have to be so tense with yourself. Let’s think about it: if you visited a family that couldn’t speak Mandarin, how would you feel? Would you feel inferior because you speak Mandarin, or would you think they’re ignorant? It’s the same thing with Shanghainese and Mandarin. As long as you find a balance between the differences and the common ground, you’ll be able to go visit them with enthusiasm and show your charm.
Thank you, what you said calmed me down a bit. But every time I see them I still feel really nervous, my whole body gets stiff. How can I relax?

When you feel this kind of pressure, try to practice more and expose yourself to more situations where people are speaking Shanghainese, and practice speaking Shanghainese more in front of people around you. That way you’ll have more chances to practice and get the hang of this “foreign language,” and you’ll gradually get used to a Shanghainese-speaking environment.
You’re right, but I’m scared of messing something up. If I say something wrong, will they think I’m being rude?

Try not to worry too much. Almost everyone makes slips of the tongue when they’re learning a new language. When they notice that you’re really trying to learn their language, they’ll actually be touched by your effort, and they won’t focus so much on your mistakes.
But what if I really get stuck, or they just can’t understand what I’m saying?

That’s really not such a big deal either. If you get stuck, you can try to get your idea across first, so they understand what you mean. If they still don’t get it, they might feel a bit unsure, but that’s okay. As long as you communicate with them in an honest and polite way, this kind of communication issue won’t affect your relationship with them.
I get it, thank you for the suggestions. But I still feel really timid and don’t know what to do.

If you’re still feeling very nervous, try taking some deep breaths and relaxing your body. Tell yourself this is an opportunity and try to look at it positively. You can also talk with your boyfriend before you go and ask him to help ease some of your tension. That might help you feel more confident.
That’s a good idea, I’ll give it a try. But if his family is very traditional and they have certain expectations of me, how should I handle that?

Sometimes you might run into that kind of situation. But don’t forget, what makes you different is also your strength. If they can see your uniqueness and appreciate it, then in their eyes you’re one of a kind. Don’t be afraid to have your own views, don’t be afraid to step out of your comfort zone, and don’t be afraid of being rejected. It’s important to hold on to your confidence and independence—that’s what matters most.
Thank you! I’ll try to talk with them and get through this period with my boyfriend’s support.
Good. Trust yourself, you’ll do really well. I hope you can gain more positive experiences from this visit!
Lately I’ve been feeling really hopeless. My thoughts are very negative, and I feel like life has no meaning.

I can understand how sad and lost you’re feeling right now. In life, we all go through times when the meaning of things feels blurry. But we can’t let that make us lose hope or stop reaching for things.
But I don’t even know what I’m supposed to be reaching for. I feel like whatever I do is meaningless.

Each of us has our own unique value and strengths. Even if you can’t find your direction for now, don’t give up on yourself so easily. And having no direction right now doesn’t mean you can’t start something new.
There’s something else that’s bothering me. I’m really afraid of losing the people around me, including my friends and family. I’m always feeling uneasy and worried.

Those feelings are normal. We all long for other people’s attention and support. But if we rely too much on others, it can make us emotionally fragile and unhealthy. We need to try to learn how to comfort and support ourselves.
I lack confidence. I always feel like I’m not doing well enough.
Actually, confidence doesn’t only come from success. We need to learn to find confidence in small things, like noticing our own strengths and good points, and trying to set goals that really fit us.
Recently I also often feel lonely, like being by myself is really lonely.

Feeling lonely is something everyone goes through, but it’s not something that can’t be worked through. Building close relationships is important, but it also helps to explore your own interests and hobbies more, and look for things that can bring you joy.
I keep feeling like people will leave me. It’s really hard for me to trust others.

That sense of distrust might be because something in the past hurt you, but we can’t let the past keep shaping our future. We need to learn to trust and listen to others, while also protecting our own boundaries.
Sometimes I feel like I’m a total failure, like no one could ever like me.

That kind of thought really isn’t realistic. Everyone has value. Maybe you don’t feel perfect right now, but we can keep working on ourselves, moving forward in a positive way, and make our lives richer and more fulfilling.
I’m really scared to face the pain from my past. It makes me feel awful.

Facing past wounds is hard, but it’s also really important. If we keep running away from them, they may keep clinging to us and affecting our lives. We need to learn to accept who we were in the past, and let ourselves grow stronger through healing.
I really want to thank you. What you’ve said to me is really helpful.
You’re very welcome. Everyone needs someone to listen and support them. We’re in this together, facing life’s difficulties side by side. Believe in yourself, and believe in the future.

My husband and I have been married for 5 years. Back then I had just graduated, I didn’t know anything, I only knew his family was pretty poor. My parents felt he treated me well, so they didn’t ask for a betrothal gift. The two of us saved up to buy an apartment and a car, and we owe more than a hundred thousand in outside debt. Now his father’s in poor health and needs surgery in Beijing, and he’s borrowed more money. The surgery went over budget and his father is still in the hospital. We’ve already spent 200,000, and every month we still have to pay 4,500 in mortgage and car loan together, and our salaries together are only around 8,000. I’m almost thirty and I want a child, but our financial situation doesn’t allow it.

I hear how troubled you are, and I can understand your anxiety. You and your husband have already gone through 5 years of marriage together, but you’ve run into some financial setbacks and pressure around caring for family, and you’re feeling discouraged because of that. At the same time, you’ve both been very strong and brave, and I want to acknowledge that attitude in you two. 

But the difficulties won’t disappear on their own, so we need to find ways to solve the problems. This isn’t something you have to carry all on your own. Right now you still have to pay 4,500 every month for the mortgage and car loan, which is a financial burden. In the time ahead, we need to think about how to work on this, because your monthly income is only around 8,000, which also means you’ve taken a big financial hit. I believe you can get through this.

I feel a lot of emotions about this, and thank you for encouraging me. But our whole family has already had no choice but to take out a bank loan and borrow money from relatives. If we have a child, we won’t be able to give them enough security in life, and that makes me feel really helpless.

What you’re thinking is very understandable; this really does sound like a very hard time. But first, we have to deal with the current debts and sort out the priorities for paying off what you owe, otherwise you can’t really make a workable plan. Second, you can think about cutting expenses to save on your monthly spending, or try to look for more sources of income. Finally, about your wish to have a child, we can explore that together. Maybe you could temporarily put that plan on hold, and wait until your financial burden has eased before you think about your dream of having a child again.

I’ll think about your suggestions and talk to my husband. But right now he’s both depressed and worried about his father’s health, and he doesn’t know what to do either. It’s really hard for us to make any decisions.

Your husband may be feeling very down and helpless right now, and that’s understandable. Nothing is more frightening than seeing a loved one in pain. But you can support him by caring about how he’s doing, talking with him patiently, and giving him some positive messages so he can regain some confidence and courage. When things don’t go as planned, we need to focus strictly on what we can control, instead of focusing on what we can’t control. That can help us manage our emotional reactions and feel more in charge. 

If your husband is feeling depressed, you can help him look into health issues and find a nutrition plan. Taking good care of your own bodies is something you both need in order to successfully deal with other problems. In addition, you can also try to find other “partners” to build the future with you, for example some professionals or other couples in a similar situation. They might be able to offer help with policies and legal matters, or a supportive supervisor who can provide more work opportunities.
The place I’ve been wanting to get into lately suddenly rejected me because of some health check indicators, so I can’t take the job. What’s going on? Why do all the bad things happen to me?

Hello. That really does sound very upsetting. How about we first take a calm look at a few questions from my side, and we can explore possible solutions step by step from there. First, when a health check becomes a barrier, it’s usually because some aspect of your physical condition doesn’t meet the organization’s standards. About this, what information have you been able to find out?
I heard that as long as you pass the medical exam you can start the job smoothly, but I’m not really clear on exactly what items they review.

Got it. Then we can go through this one by one. For the items they review, you can look them up online or in the organization’s recruitment notice, or ask the HR staff. They can tell you in detail what each item requires and how likely it is to pass. Also, the acceptance rate for new hires is something people care about, because it affects how likely you are to get this job.
It sounds really complicated. If I can’t pass, what should I do?

This situation isn’t completely hopeless. But try not to worry too much—this job isn’t your only path. Try to explore more opportunities and see which organizations focus on things that match your strengths better. While you’re looking for opportunities, it’s also important to keep a positive attitude and think more from your own perspective. In this process, you can’t rely too much on other people. After all, you’re in charge of your own life, and you’re also responsible for yourself.

What you said makes a lot of sense. I’ve always wanted to find a job that really suits me. People say, “In life, eight or nine things out of ten don’t go as we wish,” so I guess I’m not the first person to run into trouble. I’ll think about my next steps based on your suggestions.

That’s great to hear. I’m really glad I could support you. Whatever you decide to do, remember you’re not alone—there will definitely be people who support you and help you get through tough times. “Right now the situation seems boundless; the peaks near and far are hard to make out.” I believe that on your life’s path, there are many more and better things waiting for you to achieve.
A bill was passed recently. In all primary and secondary schools in France, they’ll use “Parent 1” and “Parent 2” instead of “Dad” and “Mom.” What do you think of this?

I believe every country has its own cultural differences. For our country, this may not really fit our national context. But from the perspective of equality, this change seems intended to reduce discrimination against homosexual people and allow people the freedom to choose whether being homosexual is right for them. What do you think?
I think this action isn’t about reducing discrimination. Instead, it infringes on the rights and interests of the majority.
I understand your concern. But if we can’t reduce discrimination against homosexual people, how can we truly achieve equality?
But I think this kind of protective measure is inappropriate. If in the future more and more people are homosexual, then how will humanity continue to develop?

That’s a good question. Human development has to follow the laws of nature, but we can’t exclude some people just because their sexual orientation is different from ours. Human evolution should be a way of developing that embraces diversity.
I also hope we can be inclusive of different sexual orientations. But I’m still worried about the impact of this bill.
I understand your concern. But we also can’t respond to a new cultural phenomenon with panic and exclusion. We need to maintain a rational way of thinking while also focusing on achieving equality.
I understand. Thank you for your advice.
You’re welcome. We’ll always be here to support you. If you have any confusion or need help, please feel free to contact us anytime.

My girlfriend and I both don’t come from very well-off families, but our relationship is really good, and we’re planning to get married and have children. But her parents suddenly started opposing it. They said we have to buy a home before they’ll agree. I feel really confused and helpless.

Don’t rush. Things like this usually take time and communication. First, you need to understand that your girlfriend’s parents are making this request because they care about their daughter. You can try to see it from their perspective and put yourself in their shoes.
But buying a home would be too much of a burden for us. Our family circumstances don’t allow for it. I feel really helpless and don’t know what to do.

I can understand how you feel. This really is a heavy burden. But you need to stand firm in your position and express the difficulties and limitations you’re facing, so your girlfriend’s parents can understand your situation. Have confidence, and believe that your love can overcome all the difficulties.
I want to have a good talk with my girlfriend’s parents, but I don’t know what to say to help them understand us.

First, choose an appropriate time and place, and express your feelings and hopes. Try to look at the issue from their perspective, analyze the problem, and find common ground and a way forward for both sides. Stay calm and rational during the conversation, and don’t get emotional or argue.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll try to communicate with them, and I hope there can be a good outcome.

I believe you can overcome the difficulties through your efforts and reach your goal. At the same time, remember to take care of your emotions and your health, and don’t let this issue affect your life and work. If needed, you can seek help from professional organizations to improve your ability and skills in dealing with problems.
You’re right. I’ll pay attention to keeping a calm mindset and staying healthy. Thank you for your support and help.
I really appreciate your courage and effort. Let’s hang in there together. Whatever problems you run into, you can always come talk with me.

I once found a professional counselor, but because of a work transfer, he couldn’t continue providing services for me. I found a new counselor to continue counseling, and they’ve been working with me for three months now.

I’m glad to see you actively seeking help to address your mental health concerns. Your experience shows that you have a lot of courage, and that’s the first step in moving through challenges. At the same time, right now you keep thinking about your previous counselor, and it seems like that may not be helping your recovery.
Yes, I keep thinking about my previous counselor. I know this isn’t right, but I can’t pull myself out of it.

We all have thought patterns or emotional struggles that are hard to break free from; that’s normal. You can explore this issue with your current counselor, find the root of it, and move beyond your current state. You might also consider other ways to shift the focus of your attention, such as exercise or developing other hobbies.
Mm, I want to find new interests or do some things I enjoy. But I still think of my previous counselor.

That’s normal. It’s not uncommon to feel a sense of regret around a professional counselor. But you can try to rebuild trust with your current counselor, because they can still help you get better. You can tell them about this thought and explore solutions together.
Mm, that makes me feel a bit more at ease. I’ll try to accept the current situation, and at the same time work well with my current counselor in counseling.
Okay, that’s a great idea. Accepting the situation as it is is an important part of reaching emotional balance. Building good communication with your counselor is also key to resolving the issue.
Thank you. I feel much better now than before.

I’m very glad to hear that. You’ve already taken a big step, as much as you’re able to. Keep doing this, and you’ll find that you’ll get better and better. If you still need help or have any questions, you can come to me or other professionals for support. Hang in there!

The street-stall economy has been really popular lately. It’s said that by the end of May, Chengdu had set up 2,234 temporary stall spots across the city and allowed 20,891 locations for mobile vendors, creating more than 100,000 jobs. And it’s not just Chengdu—this is becoming popular in many cities. Is this a way to help the economy recover after the pandemic? But it also feels like going back to the old street-market days. How should we look at this surge in the street-stall economy? Are we moving backward or forward?

Hello! I’m glad you’re paying attention to social issues like this. It shows that you still have a sense of responsibility toward society. The rise of the street-stall economy has indeed created some job opportunities, but at the same time, it may also bring problems like affecting the city’s image and appearance. We need to think about a direction for healthy development.
That’s true. I’ve realized that too. As citizens, we also need to start with ourselves and help keep our living environment clean and orderly. So, how do you think we should handle this issue?

We can approach it from several angles. For example, municipal management responsibilities should be put into practice, and the number and distribution of street stalls should be controlled; management of mobile stalls should be strengthened to prevent vendors from taking up the road; and the service and management standards of mobile stalls should be improved to create a brand effect. Only through the joint efforts of the government and citizens can the street-stall economy develop in a healthy and positive way.
It sounds like a process that needs everyone to work together. But when I face some of these real social issues, I feel a bit helpless, and my mood is pretty irritable.

Don’t worry. Everyone runs into upsetting things in life. You can try different ways to work through these emotions, such as adjusting your mindset and learning some psychological skills. At the same time, finding someone to talk to, sharing what’s on your mind with them, and letting out your emotions can also be a good option.
What you said makes a lot of sense. I’ll try to adjust my mindset and emotions. But work is also a bit difficult right now. What should I do?

It’s very normal to run into problems at work too. You can take the initiative to collaborate with colleagues and ask your supervisors for more guidance. Or you could try learning some work-related skills to improve your ability and competitiveness at work. Try not to get stuck in negative emotions. It’s important to keep a positive, upward-looking mindset and face challenges bravely.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll take action. I feel your encouragement and support, and it feels very warm. Thank you.

You’re welcome. I also hope I can be helpful to you. Remember to pay attention to your emotional health, keep a positive, upward-looking mindset, and believe that you can get through the difficulties and move toward a better tomorrow.

I hit the back of my head, and two nights later I started vomiting, having palpitations, and feeling panicked. I went to the hospital for a CT scan, and nothing abnormal was found. At the patient’s strong request, they gave me diazepam, and the symptoms gradually went away. Then two weeks later, similar symptoms happened again at night. I went to Anding Hospital for an examination, and the Heisman Psychological CT system showed an anxiety score of 101 and a psychoticism score of 72. Does this count as an anxiety disorder?

Hello. I understand that this situation is very troubling for you. First, you are not alone; you have us. And thank you for paying attention to your own well-being. I hear your worry about these anxiety symptoms, but try not to worry too much. I’d like to wait until you get through this point first, and then we can determine whether you have an anxiety disorder. This may take some time.
Can an anxiety disorder be diagnosed based on this one test? What if I took the test during these two weeks when I had no symptoms, and the results all came back normal?

Test results are only a reference for diagnosing an illness; we need to consider multiple factors together. I think we should first manage the symptoms and let the situation stabilize, and then consider possible treatment options.
Then how should it be judged?

We can use some optical and neuroscience techniques to observe your brain activity and chemical activity, and see whether you have an anxiety disorder. However, this will not be the only way to address the issue. We will also use other treatment approaches to ensure your overall health.
Also, could the anxiety disorder be an aftereffect of the concussion? If it was caused by this, can it be cured?

An anxiety disorder can be caused by many different factors and is not necessarily related to a concussion. We need to understand your situation further so we can arrive at a clearer diagnosis and develop an approach that is more suitable for addressing the problem.
What methods are mainly used for acute post-traumatic stress disorder?

When dealing with a traumatic event, it is very important to correctly recognize your own feelings and not hide them. We need to help the client feel safe and cared for, and encourage them to face the fact, and to express and release the emotions brought up by what happened in the past. Our goal is to help the client build an attitude that can cope with challenges, and that is very important.
What suggestions are there for counseling and treatment for chronic and delayed-onset post-traumatic stress disorder?

For chronic and delayed-onset post-traumatic stress disorder, informed treatment is very important. We need to provide clients and their family and friends with knowledge related to post-traumatic stress disorder and its treatment, and teach them how to connect with psychological support resources, such as support from relatives and from the community. It is recommended that patients receive psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy, exposure therapy, and other specialized treatment techniques.
I want to know, is it true that the stress response is divided into three stages?

The idea that the stress response is divided into three stages may apply in some situations, but it does not necessarily apply to all situations, because each person’s body and circumstances are different. If you have concerns, you can bring your questions to us and ask us to analyze and diagnose your situation in more detail. We will do our best to provide you with the most professional support and advice.
I’ve heard that anxiety disorders can be relieved through self-regulation?

Yes, anxiety disorders can be relieved through some self-regulation methods. For example, practicing deep breathing and physical relaxation techniques, becoming aware of your feelings and perceptions, and allowing yourself to gradually accept the process of emotional changes. These methods may take time and effort to practice, but we encourage you to try them, because they can help, and this is completely normal. If self-regulation does not help relieve your symptoms, you are also welcome to consult us anytime to look for more effective ways to get relief.

I left the big city some time ago, and I’ve reflected on a lot. I bought a home and a car there, and my family was in a position to help me get those two things settled. But I’ve always lived alone, and I’m not the kind of person with a strong social life. I felt very lonely. Even though I tried to analyze it rationally, I still chose to leave that place. I didn’t keep pushing myself in the industry—does that mean I’m a failure? I’m really afraid of being alone. Does that make me cowardly, not strong enough? Why can other people live so well and not be troubled by this, and take the initiative to socialize? Why can’t I do it?

I understand how you feel. First, people are born alone, so we need to learn how to be by ourselves. Relationships like family, friendships, and romantic relationships can ease some of the loneliness, but we also need to understand that being alone can be something beautiful too. Second, failure doesn’t mean you did something wrong. It’s knowing something is difficult but not daring to try, or knowing you were wrong but not daring to correct it and keep moving forward. Try not to see your current situation as a failure.
I understand, but I feel like I’m capable of doing better, yet I chose to give up because I’m afraid of loneliness.
Don’t keep putting it off—do something. Plan your life, your future direction, and bring together your experience and abilities.
Even though I have a home and a car, I feel like my life is dull and doesn’t have much meaning.

Everyone’s life is different; there are good parts and bad parts. But we can change our attitude and face things more positively, cherish life, and learn to enjoy it. For example, you can use exercise to ease anxiety and improve your mood and health.
I also want to make some genuine friends, but I don’t know how to expand my relationships.

This isn’t impossible. You can learn from How to Expand Your Relationships, or improve your emotional intelligence, so you can take the initiative to socialize appropriately and offer people what they need.
Maybe I still need time to adjust my mindset and get to know life again. Thank you for your advice. It makes me feel more confident about facing life.
Hang in there! You already have a certain level of ability. With a positive attitude and action, you’ll definitely become more confident and stronger. Remember, we’re here to support you.

I’ve run into a bit of trouble, and I don’t know how to handle it. There’s a female coworker who touches my chest every time she sees me. I feel disgusted, and I don’t feel like I can get angry, but I really don’t know how to say it without damaging the relationship.

I feel very uneasy hearing what you’ve been through. This must be really troubling for you. But I want to tell you that this is unreasonable behavior. Your wishes must be respected. If you don’t like it, please tell her directly. It’s very important to protect your own rights.
But it’s really hard for me to say it, and I don’t know how to bring it up. I’m afraid my tone might come across badly, that she’ll be unhappy, and then work will become difficult.

I can understand your distress. Suppressing your feelings can make them rebound psychologically. I suggest you first calm down and think carefully about what you want to say, then choose an appropriate time to communicate with her step by step. Make your position clear, and try to avoid expressing your emotions too intensely, so that it doesn’t create more conflict between you and affect the relationship.
Okay, I’ll try to think it through and find a good time to communicate. But I really don’t know what her intention is, or why she treats me this way.

There are many possibilities and explanations for this. Maybe she doesn’t understand what you truly want, or maybe it’s an issue on her part. But no matter what, we can’t control other people’s behavior, but we can control our own reactions and the way we handle things. As long as we have confidence and express our views firmly, we can protect our rights. We need to learn to be brave in protecting ourselves.
Thank you very much for your support and encouragement. If I encounter a situation where the reasoning isn’t on her side, do you think I can ask my leader for guidance?

Yes. If you have expressed your attitude many times and she still doesn’t change, or if her behavior crosses legal or regulatory boundaries, you can consider asking your leader for guidance or seeking professional counseling support. They may be able to offer better solutions and suggestions.
I’ll start working on it from here. Thank you for your advice and insight.
I’m very glad to be able to share my experience with you and offer you some help. You must stay strong and believe in yourself. We’ll get through this difficult time together.

Since elementary school, a lot of boys have pursued me, but even though I wasn’t against dating young, I still didn’t have any desire to be in a relationship. I asked the boys who pursued me why they liked me, and they all said they didn’t know. I don’t understand that.

Hi, I hear you’ve been having some difficulties around relationships. As young people, we should all be able to enjoy the beauty of romance in life, but everyone experiences feelings differently. You’re not against dating young, but why don’t you have the desire to be in a relationship? Are there some fears or concerns there?
Actually, I’m not afraid. I just haven’t met someone who makes me feel that way.

That’s very normal. Don’t rush it. In life, there are always a few times when the right person comes at the right time. Maybe you need to get to know more people, expand your social circle, and give yourself the chance to come into contact with more possibilities.

In college, I had four relationships. Each time, as soon as one ended, another one started. During those relationships, there were still people pursuing me, but I always felt like something was missing. I have a boyfriend now too, and although I really like him, I still feel like something is missing.

It seems like you do take relationships quite seriously, and you’re quite reflective inside. Everyone has shortcomings, and only by being accepting of each other can a relationship go further. Although your relationship experiences have had ups and downs, things with your current boyfriend seem relatively stable and comfortable. You respect and understand each other, and he’s also fairly good at taking care of you. I don’t know whether you long for a more dramatic, romantic kind of love, but even if it’s plain and ordinary, that’s okay. After all, love is more often built within the ordinary parts of life. As long as the feelings between you still exist, don’t give up too easily. Learn to cherish it.
I always feel a bit unwilling to settle. What’s missing is that feeling of “it has to be him.”

This is a very complex question. We all seek that special feeling. Sometimes what we expect isn’t necessarily what’s most real, and it’s not that all of a person’s flaws have to be mixed together before it can be called “love.” Love is made up of many different things. It may be the feeling you have when you’re together, or the growth and help the other person gives you, or even a sense of peace and security. You’ve been together for a long time. If you’re still not sure about this relationship, would you need more time to observe and understand it?
I want to understand more, but I don’t know what to do.

Okay. Then communicate more with your boyfriend, and openly share your troubles and worries. You can also learn more about some of his thoughts and wishes. I hope your relationship can move a step further. At the same time, treat yourself well too. Do things that bring you joy, develop your interests and hobbies, and increase your sense of self-worth and satisfaction.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll think it over carefully.

You’re welcome. What I’ve said is only advice; the final decision is still up to you. I hope you can stay firm in your own heart and bravely face family affection, friendship, and love. If you need it, I’ll always be here to walk alongside you. I wish you happiness and joy!

I have a wife I love very much, and she wants to divorce me. Over the past year, she’s been obsessed with the internet, and I’ve seen a lot of really intimate messages. At first, she kept asking me to forgive her, and I forgave her again and again. But later, within one year, she created five alternate QQ accounts. I found out by accident when I saw the QQ numbers and passwords written on a note. Her behavior had been very unusual. She often got up at night to use the bathroom, and once she went in, she’d stay there for half an hour or an hour. It was so cold in the middle of winter, so I started to get suspicious. One night at 3 a.m., I went to the bathroom too and saw that she was still messaging someone, and she had taken a few nude photos. I was furious and told her parents the next day. Then she ran away from home. When I got through to her on the phone, the first thing she said was, “Let’s get divorced!” I also looked into that man’s situation. He’s 10 years older than my wife. He told me my wife had deceived him too. At first she said she didn’t have a boyfriend, and when they finally met, she said she was already divorced, but actually she wasn’t. After that man found out, he also told my wife to come back. But now my wife still insists on divorce. Her dad told me she may have depression. Today he took her to get checked. When my wife first married me, she was only…

Hearing your story, I can understand the pain you’re in right now. Facing a situation like this would undoubtedly leave anyone feeling very helpless and lost. But first, what we need to do is stay calm and not act too impulsively. Your wife may find it difficult to communicate effectively with you at this point, but we can try to look at her behavior from a broader perspective.
What do you think I need to do?

First, we need to recognize that it’s very normal for difficulties to come up in a marriage. After all, if there were no difficulties, marriage might not have much meaning. When problems arise, we should shift our perspective and try to help our partner, rather than placing the blame on them. In this way, we can handle the situation better and ease the pain on both sides.
Yes… but how should I help my wife?

First, you can give her more attention and care. This is not only to help her feel valued, but also to let her know that even when problems arise, you will still support her and care for her. At the same time, we also need to understand and respect her thoughts and feelings more. Don’t ask her to do things only based on your own views and expectations, because that may only increase her pain.
I understand… thank you for your advice.

In addition, depression is one of the common mental health issues in modern society, and there are treatments for it.
